title: Alone with God (Likutey Moharan II:25)
hook: an hour a day alone with God, in your own words
tomorrow: seven beggars turn up at a wedding. why are they the gift?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebbe Nachman's good point: a little good, found and judged by, lifts a person, and lifts you. Find the good point. Today, the same rebbe on where to take your own words.

Some people talk out loud on long drives, the whole argument, both sides, nobody listening. Rebbe Nachman asked for something close to that, aimed higher. In Likutey Moharan, part two, teaching twenty-five, he says: set aside an hour or more each day, alone, somewhere private, and speak to God in your own words. Not the prayer book's Hebrew. The language you actually talk in. So yes, really. But Jewish prayer already has set words, handed down and said day after day. Which one is the real thing?
screen: `TALKING OUT LOUD ON A LONG DRIVE.` → `AN HOUR A DAY, IN YOUR OWN WORDS.` → `WHICH ONE IS THE REAL THING?`

segments.voice: First, Rebbe Nachman's case. He calls it hitbodedut, making yourself alone. Pour out what's on your heart, the way you'd talk to a true friend: what hurts, what you want, where you keep slipping. If all you can manage is one word, he says, say that one word again and again; even that is good. Set words can roll out of the mouth while the heart is somewhere else. Your own words can't. Now the other side, and it's old and strong. The Mishnah already worries about prayer that turns into a fixed chore, so the worry isn't new. But the sages also set down fixed words, and the best case for them goes like this. They hold you on the days you have no words at all. They're said together: the requests of the Amidah, the standing prayer, say heal us, forgive us, never just me. And they take you where you'd never go alone, to praise, when you only came to ask. The prayer book is bigger than your mood. Notice what Rebbe Nachman didn't do. He didn't throw out the prayer book; Breslov Hasidim pray the set services too. Hitbodedut is added on top, an hour that's yours. So the two views aren't really fighting over which prayer counts. They're weighing a balance: the words handed down to everyone, and the words only you can say.
screen: `HITBODEDUT: MAKING YOURSELF ALONE.` · `EVEN ONE WORD, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SET WORDS HOLD YOU WHEN YOU HAVE NONE.` · `ADDED ON TOP, NOT INSTEAD.` · then, large: `ALONE WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: Find the most private spot you can reach right now: a closed door, a parked car, a corner. For the sit, talk quietly, out loud, in your own everyday words; if you pray, to God, and if you don't, to the empty room. Say what's actually on your mind, and if nothing comes, say one word and let it be enough.
screen: `A CLOSED DOOR.` · `YOUR OWN WORDS, OUT LOUD.` · `ONE WORD IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Alone with God: Rebbe Nachman's hitbodedut. Time set apart each day to speak to God in your own words, in your own language.
Pocket this: alone with god, an hour that's yours beside the words handed down to everyone. Talk soon.

howItsDone: Breslov Hasidim practice hitbodedut, speaking to God alone in their own words, often outdoors or in a quiet room, alongside the set daily prayers of the siddur.

sources.ref: Likutey Moharan II:25 (hitbodedut: set aside an hour or more daily, alone, to speak to God in one's own language; even a single word repeated is good)
Mishnah Berakhot 4:4 (Rabbi Eliezer: one who makes his prayer keva, fixed, his prayer is not supplication)

notes: Likutey Moharan II:25 paraphrased: an hour or more daily of hitbodedut, in a private place, in one's own language, pouring out one's heart as to a good friend; if one can say only one word, repeat it, and that too is very good. Confirm that the one-word point is in II:25 (it may be from Sichot HaRan or Likutey Etzot).

Mishnah Berakhot 4:4 paraphrased. 'The sages also set down fixed words': the set prayers (Berakhot 26b; 33a). 'The requests of the Amidah say heal us, forgive us': the plural petitions of the weekday Amidah; confirm framing.
'Breslov Hasidim pray the set services too' is offered as general knowledge; confirm.

Debate shape: Rebbe Nachman's case for your own words and the best case for fixed liturgy are each given in their own terms; the fork asks for the prayer book's best case. Practice kind: say it out loud. The 'if you pray… if you don't…' framing is used here and nowhere else in 1611–1617.
